title: Jeremiah 11:1–17
context: The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah (11:1) to proclaim “the words of this covenant” to Judah and Jerusalem. The LORD recalls the covenant made at the exodus, with its curse on the one who does not hear (11:3, echoing Deuteronomy 27:26 by reference), and Jeremiah answers, “Amen, LORD” (11:5). The LORD then exposes a conspiracy: Judah has returned to the sins of its ancestors and broken the covenant (11:9–13). Some readers connect this covenant preaching with Josiah’s reform (2 Kings 22–23), though the text does not say so. In 11:14 the LORD tells Jeremiah not to pray for this people (compare 7:16 and 14:11). On how prayer relates to God’s purpose, see the existing box at Joshua 10:14 rather than a new one here.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s message originates with God, not with his own reflection, and that he is called to speak it faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula as marking divine authority behind what follows. Both traditions read the verse as introducing a covenant sermon, grounded in revelation and delivered through a chosen messenger.

verses.text: “Hear the words of this covenant, and speak to the men of Judah, and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to hear the words of this covenant and speak them to Judah and Jerusalem. Arminian readers see the covenant renewed in preaching, calling the people to respond anew.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the covenant as God’s gracious arrangement with his people, now pressed upon a faithless generation. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a summons to covenant faithfulness, addressed to the whole community.

verses.text: and say to them, the LORD, the God of Israel says: ‘Cursed is the man who doesn’t hear the words of this covenant,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD declares cursed anyone who does not hear the words of this covenant. Arminian readers note the echo of Deuteronomy 27:26 by reference, and the real consequences attached to refusing God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the curse as part of the covenant’s sanctions, which Israel had accepted. Both traditions read the verse as showing that covenant privilege brings accountability, and that hearing means obeying.

verses.text: which I commanded your fathers in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the iron furnace,’ saying, ‘Obey my voice and do them, according to all which I command you; so you shall be my people, and I will be your God;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD recalls commanding their fathers when he brought them out of Egypt, the iron furnace: obey my voice, so you shall be my people and I your God. Arminian readers see covenant relationship joined to obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the formula, my people and your God, as the heart of the covenant, given in grace after redemption from Egypt. Shared ground: both traditions read the order, rescue then command, as showing that obedience responds to grace.

verses.text: that I may establish the oath which I swore to your fathers, to give them a land flowing with milk and honey,’ as it is today.” Then I answered, and said, “Amen, LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes: God’s purpose was to establish the oath sworn to their fathers, the land flowing with milk and honey, and Jeremiah answers, Amen, LORD. Arminian readers see the prophet’s personal assent to the covenant’s terms.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness to his promise to the patriarchs. Both traditions read Jeremiah’s Amen as agreement with God’s word, including its blessings and curses, and they note that the land had indeed been given.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “Proclaim all these words in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, saying, ‘Hear the words of this covenant, and do them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah to proclaim these words in Judah’s cities and Jerusalem’s streets: hear and do. Arminian readers see a public call to obedience, extended widely so that no one could claim ignorance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the proclamation as God’s means of confronting the people with their covenant duty. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as joining hearing and doing, a recurring theme in Scripture.

verses.text: For I earnestly protested to your fathers in the day that I brought them up out of the land of Egypt, even to this day, rising early and protesting, saying, “Obey my voice.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he earnestly warned their fathers from the exodus until now, rising early and protesting. Arminian readers see God’s persistent, patient appeal, which shows his real desire for the people’s obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repeated warnings as underscoring Israel’s guilt, since they were warned again and again. Both traditions read rising early as an image of God’s diligent, untiring call to his people.

verses.text: Yet they didn’t obey, nor turn their ear, but everyone walked in the stubbornness of their evil heart. Therefore I brought on them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do, but they didn’t do them.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Yet they did not obey, but walked in the stubbornness of their evil heart, so the LORD brought the covenant’s words upon them. Arminian readers stress that judgment follows the people’s persistent refusal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the stubborn heart as the deep source of disobedience, needing the new heart later promised (compare 31:33). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as covenant sanctions justly applied after long patience.

verses.text: The LORD said to me, “A conspiracy is found among the men of Judah, and among the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah that a conspiracy is found among Judah and Jerusalem. Arminian readers see the word conspiracy as showing that the people’s turning away was deliberate and shared, a collective decision.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conspiracy as organized rebellion against God, exposed by his all-seeing knowledge. Both traditions read the verse as a sober charge that unfaithfulness had become a common, almost planned, way of life.

verses.text: They have turned back to the iniquities of their forefathers, who refused to hear my words. They have gone after other gods to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have broken my covenant which I made with their fathers.
verses.arminianNotes: They returned to their forefathers’ iniquities, served other gods, and broke the covenant. Arminian readers note the word returned, suggesting a reform reversed, as people went back to old ways after a time of change.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as naming both houses, Israel and Judah, as covenant breakers. Shared ground: both traditions read the charge as idolatry and covenant breach, and they hold any link to a specific reform as uncertain.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on them which they will not be able to escape; and they will cry to me, but I will not listen to them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will bring evil they cannot escape, and when they cry he will not listen. Arminian readers see a time when persistent rejection reaches its consequence, and late cries no longer avert judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s refusal to hear as judicial, a response to long hardness. Both traditions read the verse soberly, and they note that elsewhere Jeremiah still holds out hope for those who seek God with all their heart (compare 29:13).

verses.text: Then the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry to the gods to which they offer incense, but they will not save them at all in the time of their trouble.
verses.arminianNotes: The people will cry to the gods they burn incense to, but those gods will not save them in their trouble. Arminian readers see the bitter irony: the gods they chose prove useless at the moment of need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing idols’ inability to save, contrasting them with the LORD who alone delivers. Shared ground: both traditions read the line as a warning against trusting anything other than the living God.

verses.text: For according to the number of your cities are your gods, Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem you have set up altars to the shameful thing, even altars to burn incense to Baal.’
verses.arminianNotes: Judah’s gods are as many as its cities, and Jerusalem’s altars to the shameful thing as many as its streets. Arminian readers see how widespread idolatry had become, filling the land with rival loyalties.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that shameful thing is a scornful name for Baal, exposing the disgrace of such worship. Both traditions read the verse as describing pervasive idolatry, offered openly throughout Judah and Jerusalem.

verses.text: “Therefore don’t pray for this people. Don’t lift up cry or prayer for them; for I will not hear them in the time that they cry to me because of their trouble.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells Jeremiah not to pray or cry for this people, for he will not hear them in their trouble. Arminian readers see a dramatic sign of how far the people have gone, with intercession itself set aside (compare 7:16; 14:11).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the command as God’s sovereign decision that judgment will proceed. Shared ground: both traditions agree that God truly hears prayer; on how prayer relates to his purpose, see the existing keyContrast at Joshua 10:14 rather than a new one here.

verses.text: What has my beloved to do in my house, since she has behaved lewdly with many, and the holy flesh has passed from you? When you do evil, then you rejoice.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks what his beloved has to do in his house, having acted lewdly, and rejoicing when doing evil. Arminian readers note the tender word beloved, showing God’s love even while confronting unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as exposing worship in the temple that is empty because of continued sin. Both traditions read the line as a rebuke of religion without repentance; the wording of this verse is difficult, and its details are not pressed.

verses.text: The LORD called your name, “A green olive tree, beautiful with goodly fruit.” With the noise of a great roar he has kindled fire on it, and its branches are broken.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD once named Judah a green olive tree with goodly fruit, but now kindles fire on it and breaks its branches. Arminian readers see a reversal of blessing when fruitfulness turns to faithlessness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as God’s sovereign right to plant and to judge, compare Romans 11:17–24 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the olive tree as a picture of Israel’s privilege and the seriousness of its loss.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you, because of the evil of the house of Israel and of the house of Judah, which they have done to themselves in provoking me to anger by offering incense to Baal.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies, who planted Judah, has pronounced evil against them because of their incense to Baal. Arminian readers note that the people provoked God by their own deeds, bringing harm on themselves.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the planter’s authority to judge what he planted, and Israel’s guilt in its idolatry. Both traditions read the phrase which they have done to themselves as stressing that judgment is the fruit of their own choices.
